prompt.context: Your client is RX Co, a pharmacy retailer with stores across the United States. To bolster their presence in the Pacific Northwest, they are in talks with Drug Corp to purchase retail assets in the region. Though the acquisition seems sound, the RX Co CEO wants to be sure that the transaction will help them achieve growth.
prompt.question: Can you help the company evaluate the deal?

clarifying_info.q: What is RX Co's specific growth goal?
clarifying_info.a: RX Co aims to grow annual revenue by 20% from current levels, and they want this to happen in the first year after the acquisition is complete.

clarifying_info.q: When would the acquisition be completed and stores operational?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the acquisition can be completed and the assets operational in one year.

clarifying_info.q: Does RX Co have stores in the Pacific Northwest already?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. RX Co has 5,000 stores in the NW region; Drug Corp has 900 stores in the NW region.

clarifying_info.q: Can we assume NW region stores have the same revenue makeup as nationwide stores?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, you can assume stores in the NW region have the same revenue makeup and average overall revenue as stores nationwide.

exhibits.title: RX Co and Drug Corp Store Metrics
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of RX Co and Drug Corp showing pharmacy revenue percentage, front-of-house merchandise revenue percentage, overall revenue per day per store, and total US store count.

framework: Clarify the specific growth target (revenue, not profit) and timeline (Year 1 post-acquisition)
Identify revenue streams for pharmacy retailers: Pharmacy (RX) revenue and Front-of-House merchandise revenue
Quantify RX Co's current NW region revenue baseline (NW stores only, not all US stores)
Calculate the revenue target implied by the 20% growth goal
Calculate incremental revenue that the Drug Corp NW store acquisition would add
Compare incremental revenue to revenue gap; conclude whether the deal achieves the target
Discuss qualitative risks and other levers to close any gap

questions.prompt: Calculate RX Co's current annual pharmacy revenue for the NW region, determine the 20% growth target, and then calculate the incremental pharmacy revenue the Drug Corp NW acquisition would add. Does the acquisition close the gap?
questions.guidance: Candidate should focus only on NW stores (not all US). Must use pharmacy revenue share (70%) times daily revenue times 365 days times NW store count. Should compare incremental revenue from acquisition to required growth. A strong candidate will also note the exact shortfall and how many Drug Corp stores would be needed.

math.setup: Current NW pharma rev = 70% x $11,000/day x 365 days/year x 5,000 NW stores. Growth target = current NW pharma rev x 1.20 (or equivalently, find the $gap = current x 0.20). Acquisition pharma rev = 70% x $7,800/day x 365 days/year x 900 NW stores.
steps: Current NW pharma rev = 0.7 x $11,000 x 365 x 5,000 = ~$14.0B
Interviewer guidance notes target as $14B x 1.15 = ~$16.1B (using 15% increment for pharma only as a simplification); candidates may also compute $14B x 1.20 = $16.8B depending on interpretation
Incremental pharma rev from acquisition = 0.7 x $7,800 x 365 x 900 = ~$1.8B
Conclusion: the acquisition adds only ~$1.8B against a ~$2.8B needed increment — the deal alone does NOT achieve the 20% revenue growth target
math.answer: The Drug Corp acquisition adds approximately $1.8B in annual NW pharmacy revenue, which falls short of the ~$2.8B increment needed to hit a 20% growth target. The deal will not achieve RX Co's revenue growth goal in Year 1.

questions.prompt: What else should be considered when evaluating or calculating the additional revenue RX Co can achieve through Drug Corp acquisitions?
questions.guidance: Candidate should raise factors that could reduce or inflate the incremental revenue estimate: sales cannibalization, sales retention risk, pricing changes.

brainstorming.prompt: What else should be considered when evaluating or calculating the additional revenue RX Co can achieve through Drug Corp acquisitions?

categories.name: Revenue Leakage Risks
ideas: Sales cannibalization: acquiring stores in the same region may shift customers between stores rather than adding net new revenue
Sales retention: Drug Corp customers have brand loyalty; converting stores to RX Co brand may cause customer attrition

categories.name: Revenue Upside Levers
ideas: Increasing retail pricing of RX items post-acquisition
Cross-selling front-of-house merchandise to newly acquired customer base
Acquiring more Drug Corp stores beyond the 900 NW stores to close the revenue gap

categories.name: Operational / Regulatory Risks
ideas: Delays in acquisition and store conversion due to DEA license transfers, liquor license transfers
IT, HR, accounting, and back-office systems integration delays
Consumer backlash if pricing is increased

recommendation: Do not proceed with the acquisition as currently structured if the sole objective is achieving 20% revenue growth in Year 1
Even under optimistic assumptions (no cannibalization, 100% sales retention), the 900 NW Drug Corp stores add only ~$1.8B in pharmacy revenue against a ~$2.8B gap — a meaningful shortfall
If growth is the priority, RX Co should explore acquiring more Drug Corp stores, entering other markets, or pursuing organic growth strategies
risks: Sales cannibalization from overlapping NW store footprints
Customer attrition due to brand conversion from Drug Corp to RX Co
DEA license and regulatory approval delays pushing operational timeline beyond Year 1
Consumer backlash from potential post-acquisition price increases
next_steps: Determine how many Drug Corp stores (beyond 900) would need to be acquired to close the full revenue gap
Assess feasibility of full Drug Corp NW portfolio acquisition
Evaluate alternative growth strategies: organic expansion, other regional acquisitions, pricing strategy
Conduct integration planning for DEA licenses, brand conversion, and systems
